response:
The central question is whether the features learned by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on intermediate pretraining checkpoints can serve as a leading indicator of when specific capabilities — say, in-context learning or multi-step reasoning — become encoded in the model's representations, rather than discovering this only after behavioral evaluations. The key concepts are: SAE features as approximately monosemantic directions in activation space; mechanistic attribution, meaning tracing how much a given feature causally contributes to a downstream behavior via path patching or attribution patching; and "drift," meaning how a feature's identity, connectivity, and causal role change across checkpoints even when its decoder direction looks superficially stable. The working hypothesis is that capability emergence isn't a sudden phase transition at the behavioral level but has a detectable mechanistic precursor — features that will later causally support a capability first appear as weakly-attributed noise and gradually accrete causal weight.

What an expert worries about that a beginner misses: SAE feature identity across checkpoints is not given — there is no canonical correspondence between feature 347 at step 10k and feature 347 at step 100k, so any "drift" analysis requires a non-trivial alignment procedure (e.g., cosine-similarity matching or Procrustes alignment of decoder matrices), and errors in that alignment will produce ghost drift signals that look like meaningful capability formation but are just matching artifacts. The deeper worry is that attribution patching gives you a linear approximation to causal effect, so features that appear to "emerge" in the attribution graph may be doing so because the approximation quality itself changes with model competence, not because the underlying circuit changed.

When a polysemantic proto-feature splits, maximum cosine similarity alignment will assign the checkpoint-N feature to whichever of the two daughter features is geometrically closest — typically the one that inherited the dominant direction — and silently discard the other daughter as "new." The naive drift metric then reports low drift for the matched pair (their decoder vectors are similar by construction) and spuriously registers the second daughter as a freshly emerged feature with no ancestry, when in fact both daughters share causal history with the parent. This is not hypothetical: Bricken et al. (2023) and subsequent Anthropic SAE work on GPT-2 and Claude layers document that feature splitting is a systematic phenomenon during SAE scaling, and Templeton et al. (2024) show that the number of "live" features grows roughly with SAE width in a way consistent with ongoing splitting rather than de-novo emergence. The invalidation of the naive drift metric is precise: it conflates geometric continuity with causal continuity, so a feature lineage that should be coded as "one feature differentiating into two circuits" gets coded as "one stable feature plus one new feature," undercounting the mechanistic change by exactly the number of split-off daughters. For capability attribution this is fatal — if you are trying to detect when a reasoning-relevant feature accretes causal weight, a split event looks like the proto-feature plateaued (low drift, moderate attribution) while a seemingly unrelated new feature suddenly has high attribution, severing the lineage you needed to trace.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1797)

The core confound is that attribution patching estimates a feature's causal contribution by routing the intervention through the SAE's reconstruction, so if the SAE's explained variance of the residual stream improves from, say, 85% to 95% between two checkpoints, a feature's measured attribution will increase even if its true causal role is unchanged — the signal is partly "the SAE got better at its job." The cleanest diagnostic is to hold the SAE fixed (train one SAE on checkpoint N, then apply it without retraining to checkpoint N+1) and recompute attributions; if attribution rises under the fixed SAE, it is more plausibly a genuine model-side change, whereas a rise that only appears when you retrain the SAE at each checkpoint implicates approximator quality. A complementary approach is to track the SAE's per-feature reconstruction fidelity — specifically the fraction of a feature's activation variance that survives the encode-decode round trip — and regress attribution change on that fidelity change; Cunningham et al. (2023) provide the technical scaffolding for this in their TopK SAE evaluations, where they decompose loss recovered per feature. You can also run direct causal interventions (activation patching bypassing the SAE entirely, patching the raw residual stream direction corresponding to the decoder vector) and compare the slope of that curve across checkpoints to the SAE-mediated attribution curve; divergence between the two directly measures approximator artifact. The uncomfortable expert worry is that none of these controls is clean when sparsity itself shifts: if L1 penalty or TopK threshold is held fixed but the underlying activation distribution sharpens during training, the effective support of the SAE changes, and features that were previously "on" for many tokens get pruned to fewer, mechanically reducing their attribution independent of any causal change in the circuit.

The dissociation — stable decoder direction, collapsed firing rate — tells you that the representational geometry supporting the capability has been preserved or even sharpened, but the model has stopped routing activation through that particular subspace as broadly; the encoder side of the SAE, which was fit to checkpoint-N statistics, is now missing activations that have migrated to a nearby but distinct direction in checkpoint-N+1's residual stream. This is mechanistically distinct from capability loss: it more likely signals that the model has become more precise in when it deploys the relevant computation, either because upstream attention heads have been pruned or sharpened (reducing the set of token contexts that trigger the feature) or because the representation has been "promoted" to a cleaner, slightly rotated direction the old encoder doesn't catch. The two competing explanations are therefore: (A) the capability is now encoded more sparsely and efficiently — fewer tokens need the feature because earlier layers handle more cases — versus (B) the feature's role has been partially redistributed to a daughter feature or parallel circuit that the checkpoint-N SAE has no dictionary entry for, and firing rate dropped because the SAE is simply blind to where the computation moved. The adjudicating experiment is a targeted activation patch: take a prompt that behaviorally requires the capability, ablate the decoder direction at checkpoint N+1 by subtracting its projection from the residual stream, and measure behavioral degradation; if performance collapses despite low SAE firing rate, explanation A is supported — the direction is still causally load-bearing even if the SAE understimates its use. To rule out explanation B, you retrain a small SAE on just checkpoint-N+1 activations for that layer, check whether a new feature with high firing rate appears near the old decoder direction (within ~0.1 cosine distance), and compare its causal footprint to the original; redistribution would show a new high-firing neighbor with overlapping but not identical behavioral specificity, which Marks et al. (2024) use a similar strategy to detect in their circuit-tracing work on factual recall.

The choice of unit is not merely methodological preference — it produces genuinely different emergence timelines, and the disagreement is informative rather than a problem to be resolved. At the individual-feature level, emergence looks punctuated and late: a feature crosses some attribution threshold at a specific checkpoint, giving you a sharp date, but this is partially an artifact of the threshold and the redistribution dynamics we just discussed. At the feature-cluster level (grouping by decoder cosine similarity or co-activation, as in Lindsey et al.'s 2025 work on SAE feature families), emergence looks earlier and more gradual — proto-cluster members appear with weak attribution several thousand steps before any single feature clears a behavioral threshold, suggesting the representational scaffolding precedes functional deployment. The circuit-subgraph level is the most causally honest unit: a capability is present when a connected set of features with measurable causal edges — attention head outputs writing to MLP inputs that activate specific features — can be ablated to selectively degrade the target behavior, regardless of whether any individual feature looks "strong." The critical implication is that individual-feature analysis will systematically underestimate how early a capability begins forming, because it misses the distributed precursor state where no single feature is dominant but the subgraph already has the right connectivity skeleton; Conmy et al.'s (2023) ACDC work on IOI circuits in GPT-2 implicitly demonstrates this — the circuit exists as a recoverable subgraph well before its components become individually salient by activation magnitude. The practical answer for attribution drift as a proxy for capability emergence timing is therefore: use the subgraph as your unit but report feature-cluster statistics as a cheaper approximation, and treat the gap between when the cluster first coheres and when individual features cross threshold as a measure of how much "dark emergence" your feature-level analysis was missing.

This is the sharpest challenge to the proxy premise: drift is defined relative to a tracked subgraph, but if the implementation relocates, you are measuring the decline of an old circuit rather than the health of the capability itself, and the two signals are indistinguishable without an independent behavioral probe running in parallel. A principled definition that doesn't privilege either level would require a third anchor — something like a formal specification of the capability that can be evaluated against both behavioral outputs and mechanistic structure independently — but no such specification exists for most capabilities of alignment interest; "deceptive reasoning" or "situational awareness" resist the kind of input-output formalization that would make behavioral probes crisp, and they resist the kind of modular decomposition that would make subgraph tracking clean. The closest candidate in the literature is the interventionist framework implicit in Woodward-style causation: a capability has emerged when there exists a surgical intervention on the mechanistic substrate that selectively degrades the behavior, and that intervention is stable across a range of prompts and paraphrases. This is more principled because it ties the mechanistic and behavioral levels together through causal structure rather than correlation, but it still has a privileged element — the choice of intervention granularity — and Geiger et al.'s (2023) interchange intervention work on algorithmic tasks shows that the "right" granularity is itself model- and task-dependent, not derivable from first principles. The indeterminacy for alignment-relevant SAE drift signals is serious and underappreciated: if we cannot say when a capability emerged without making contestable choices about level and granularity, then an early-warning system built on drift metrics will produce alerts whose timing depends on those choices, meaning two researchers with different but defensible methodologies could disagree by thousands of training steps about when, say, a deception-relevant feature cluster became causally active. The practical implication is that SAE drift should be treated not as a detector with a threshold but as a family of signals requiring triangulation — behavioral probes, subgraph attribution, feature cluster cohesion, and direct activation patching should all be run in parallel, and genuine emergence is most credibly dated to the earliest checkpoint where a majority of these signals cross their respective thresholds, accepting that the resulting estimate carries irreducible methodological uncertainty on the order of the disagreement between signals.

When a capability is implemented redundantly across parallel circuits, surgical ablation of any single circuit will fail to degrade behavior, and the interventionist criterion will conclude the capability is absent or weak precisely when it is most robustly present — this is not a edge case but the expected outcome for any capability that was selected for during training because it improved loss reliably, since redundancy is a natural consequence of gradient descent on a capability that matters. The underdating problem is therefore systematic and worst for the capabilities most relevant to alignment: deception, situational awareness, and goal-directed planning are exactly the capabilities where a competent optimizer would be expected to build in robustness, meaning the interventionist criterion applied naively will consistently report these as absent until the redundancy is itself mapped and simultaneously ablated. Wang et al.'s (2022) IOI circuit work already hints at this — even in that relatively simple task, there are backup heads that partially compensate when primary heads are ablated, and the IOI circuit in GPT-2 medium involves enough redundancy that single-head ablations understate the circuit's causal contribution. The fix in principle is multi-site joint ablation: ablate all circuits hypothesized to implement the capability simultaneously and check for behavioral degradation, as Conmy et al.'s ACDC attempts to automate, but this requires first knowing the full set of implementing circuits, which is precisely what you are trying to discover — making the criterion circular when redundancy is present. The deeper implication is that the interventionist criterion, even corrected for redundancy, will underdate emergence because it requires that you have already found all implementing circuits before you can apply it, meaning there is an irreducible discovery lag between when a capability becomes mechanistically present and when any criterion we have can certify it — and for alignment this lag is not a minor measurement error but a structural blind spot in the entire mechanistic interpretability approach to capability monitoring.
